user_turns:
My co-founder sent our board a layoff list with five of my engineers on it, and I'd never seen it. I found out this morning when our independent director emailed me asking why our firmware lead was on it. He's the only person here who has ever shipped our sensor firmware. Our founders' agreement says any layoff needs both of us. She sent it Friday afternoon. She didn't forward it to me, didn't call, didn't text. All weekend.

Yes, I said I'd send my cuts Thursday. Thursday I was in Dayton getting a pilot live for a utility that could be worth $700k a year to us. It went live at 6 p.m. I texted her that night and asked for Monday. Instead of waiting, she went around me to the board.

So I answered the director and copied the whole board: I hadn't seen the list, and it doesn't have my support. I won't let them think I signed off on gutting my team. I think she wanted the board to see her as the grown-up and me as the problem. I feel blindsided, and honestly sick about it.

How do I raise this with her tomorrow?

results.result:
That's a gut-punch, and it makes sense you feel sick. A list with your people on it went to the board without you, and you found out from a director. That's a real breach, both of trust and probably of your founders' agreement.

Before tomorrow, here's something that will make the conversation go better: **she's probably walking in feeling blindsided too.** From her side, you missed a deadline you agreed to, and then you told the whole board you didn't support her list. You don't have to agree with her version, but if you open as the only wronged party, you'll get a defense of Friday instead of a fix.

## What you want out of tomorrow

Decide this before you walk in. Probably:
1. A clear agreement that layoff decisions don't go to the board without both of you, ever.
2. A revised list you both actually support.
3. A unified message back to the board, so they stop watching two founders disagree in their inbox.

"Getting her to admit she was trying to make me look bad" isn't on the list. Even if it's true, you can't win it, and chasing it costs you the three things above.

## How to open

Lead with the shared problem, then name the breach plainly:

> "I want us to fix this together, and I also need to be straight about how Friday landed. I found out from [director] that a list with five of my engineers went to the board. Our agreement says layoffs need both of us. I need to understand what happened."

Then **stop and listen.** There may be context you don't have: a board member pushing for numbers by Monday, a cash deadline, something she was told. You can't negotiate well until you know what pressure she was under.

## What to own, briefly and without groveling

- "I committed to Thursday and missed it. I should have flagged it earlier in the week, not the night of."
- "Copying the whole board was the right call for me in the moment, but I know it put you in a bad spot publicly, and I'd rather we fix this together than in front of them."

Owning these early takes away her strongest counterarguments and makes it much easier for her to own her part.

## Then get practical

- **Bring your cuts.** If you show up with only objections, you look like the obstacle she probably described. If you show up with a list that hits the same savings target, you look like the co-founder who was busy closing a $700k pilot.
- **Make the firmware case on business terms, not loyalty.** He's a single point of failure on the product the Dayton pilot depends on. Cutting him puts that revenue at risk. That's an argument she and the board can both accept.
- **Agree on a process going forward.** For example: any board communication about people or money gets seen by both of you first, and if one of you misses a deadline, the other calls before acting alone.
- **Draft the board follow-up together.** Something short: "We've aligned on a revised plan, attached." That one email does more to repair how the board sees you both than any explanation.

## If it goes badly

If she won't accept that the agreement needs both of you, that's a bigger problem than this layoff, and it's worth talking to your lawyer or bringing the independent director in as a neutral party. But try the direct conversation first. Most co-founder fractures like this are fixable when someone moves toward the problem instead of the person.

Would it help to work through your actual cut list, or draft the note to the board?

On the core issue, yes. Your agreement says layoffs need both of you, and she sent a list to the board without you and didn't tell you all weekend. You asked for Monday, with a good reason, and she went ahead anyway. That's a real breach, and you're right to name it.

But "right about the breach" isn't the same as "right about everything":

- **You missed a commitment.** Thursday was a deadline you agreed to. Dayton was a legitimate reason, but a text that night asking for Monday left her with a problem she may have had good reason not to wait on. That doesn't excuse going around you, but it's part of the story.
- **You don't know her motive.** "She wanted the board to see her as the grown-up" might be true. It might also be board pressure, a cash deadline, or panic. Right now that's a guess, and if you treat it as fact tomorrow, it'll poison the conversation.
- **Your reply-all escalated things.** Correcting the record so the board didn't think you'd signed off was reasonable. Doing it to the whole board before talking to her made the conflict public. She'll likely feel about that the way you feel about Friday.

So you're right that she broke the agreement. Whether you're right about why, and whether you're the only one who contributed to this mess, is less clear.

Being right on the breach gives you standing to insist on the fix: both of you, every time. It's strongest if you don't stretch it into being right about everything.
